results.note: Search, criteria, PROSPERO, flow (6389-2218=4171; 214; 89; 69 excluded; 20) and counts match. Recounted: 16 distinct studies, 5 fair and 11 poor across Tables 1-4; no good. Meta-analysis reasons as Discussion 7th paragraph.

results.corrected_extracted: Two case-control studies and one cohort, all rated fair. UK GAP study (410 patients with first-episode psychosis, 370 controls from the same area): against never-use, skunk-type use adjusted odds ratio 2.91 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.60), hash-type 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77), daily skunk-type use 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30); onset about 4 years earlier with higher- than with lower-potency use (hazard ratio 1.68, 1.08 to 2.63; adjusted for gender and frequency of use). EU-GEI study (901 patients and 1,237 population controls in England, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain and Brazil): types of 10% THC or more against never-use 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2), under 10% 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5); daily use 4.8 (2.5 to 6.3) and 2.2 (1.4 to 3.6). Both adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco, alcohol and other drugs. UK cohort of 256 patients after a first episode: 58% of those who continued daily use of higher-potency cannabis relapsed within 2 years against 24% of those who had used cannabis in the past (adjusted odds ratio 3.28, 1.22 to 9.18); lower-potency or infrequent higher-potency use 1.82 (0.36 to 8.75); adjusted for alcohol, other illicit drugs, cigarettes, care intensity at onset and medication adherence. None of these three studies looked at concentrates as a separate form.
results.note: All numbers match text and Table 1 image. The onset hazard ratio compares higher- with lower-potency users, not never-use, and was adjusted for gender and frequency (Results 7th paragraph); named now.

results.corrected_extracted: Studies of concentrates and one of liquid or resin cannabis, all cross-sectional and rated poor. 20-country online survey of 181,870 (self-report with pictorial aids; adjusted for age, gender, sexual orientation, education and other substance use), butane hash oil against lower-potency herbal cannabis: self-reported lifetime psychosis diagnosis 1.11 (0.85 to 1.46), anxiety diagnosis 1.80 (1.60 to 2.01; 1.72, 1.55 to 1.91, against higher-potency herbal), depression diagnosis 1.34 (1.21 to 1.48; 1.15, 1.03 to 1.25, against higher-potency herbal). US sample of 156: higher-potency concentrate use and psychosis symptoms r 0.11 (-0.20 to 0.40), anxiety 0.21 (-0.10 to 0.49), depression 0.17 (-0.15 to 0.45). US sample of 191, frequent concentrate against frequent herbal use: anxiety means 1.1 and 0.66, depression 0.72 and 0.76, no significant difference. Within-person survey of 574 people who used cannabis in the past year, mostly infrequently: psychosis-like experiences mean 1.1 with concentrates and 1.2 with herbal cannabis (0 to 10 scale; Cohen's d 0.12). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders, liquid or resin against dry or herbal cannabis: residual or late-onset psychotic disorder odds ratio 0.212 (0.061 to 0.735), which Table 1 labels no association.
results.note: Numbers and minus signs match Tables 1, 3, 4. The review gives the 156-sample r values for higher-potency concentrate use, not concentrate use; it never calls the Japanese liquid or resin cannabis a concentrate; comparator is 'dry or herbal'.

results.corrected_extracted: Anxiety, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): generalised anxiety disorder more likely with higher- than with lower-potency use in a UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (odds ratio 1.92, 1.11 to 3.32; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, depression score at 13 and frequency; rated fair); no difference between higher- and lower-potency herbal cannabis in the 20-country survey (1.05, 0.98 to 1.12). Depression, four cross-sectional studies (one fair): a slight increase in the 20-country survey (higher- against lower-potency herbal 1.18, 1.11 to 1.25) and little evidence in the UK sample (higher- against lower-potency 1.28, 0.68 to 2.32). Studies of people using medical cannabis (four for anxiety: one cross-sectional, rated fair, and three repeated-measures, rated poor; three repeated-measures studies for depression, all poor) gave varied results that the authors call hard to interpret. The authors conclude there is some evidence for anxiety and little for depression.
results.note: Numbers, adjustments and ratings match. Added the lower-potency comparator for both UK-sample results and the designs of the medical cannabis studies (Results 16th-18th, 22nd paragraphs; Tables 3-4).

results.corrected_extracted: Systematic review of observational studies (MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO to 14 January 2021; PROSPERO CRD42021226447) comparing higher- with lower-potency cannabis as each study defined it. Six cross-sectional studies examined cannabis use disorder: one rated fair and five poor on a modified Newcastle-Ottawa Scale, for limits in the measure of exposure in all six and in outcome measures, sample selection and confounder adjustment in the poor ones. Exposure was self-reported in all six. Outcomes: Severity of Dependence Scale (two annual drug surveys; 0 to 15, cut-off 3 or more), Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (UK sample of 1,087), MINI cannabis screening test (US sample of 191), a self-report questionnaire (US sample of 156) and an ICD-10 clinical interview (71 Japanese patients).

results.corrected_extracted: UK annual drug survey 2009-10 (2,514; skunk against grass and resin; adjusted for gender and age; poor): each extra day a month of higher-potency use went with a Severity of Dependence Scale score 0.254 higher (95% CI 0.161 to 0.357 in Table 2; 0.161 to 0.3578 in the text), with no association for grass (0.020, -0.029 to 0.070) or resin (0.025, -0.019 to 0.067). Survey of 55,240 people in 175 countries 2017-18 (adjusted for age, gender, amount and frequency of use and tobacco added; poor): the classes using sinsemilla and herbal (b 0.155, 0.100 to 0.209) and hashish and herbal (b 0.262, 0.188 to 0.337) scored higher than the herbal cannabis class. UK sample of 1,087 aged about 24 (Cannabis Abuse Screening Test; adjusted for sex, childhood socio-economic position, age at first use and frequency; fair): recent cannabis problems with higher- than with lower-potency use, odds ratio 4.08 (1.41 to 11.81). 71 Japanese patients with cannabis-related disorders (ICD-10 interview; no adjustment listed; poor): liquid or resin against dry or herbal cannabis, dependence syndrome 6.850 (1.866 to 25.145 in Table 2; 6.9, 1.19 to 25.15, in the text).
results.note: All numbers and minus signs match Table 2 and text. Changed: 'online' not in review (annual drug survey); named lower-potency comparator for the 4.08; comparator class is 'herbal cannabis', not 'herbal only'; 'dry or herbal'.

results.corrected_extracted: US sample of 156 people (self-report questionnaire; no adjustment listed; poor): higher-potency herbal use and use-disorder symptoms r 0.09 (-0.12 to 0.30); for higher-potency concentrate use the review prints -0.05 (-0.35 to -0.26), an interval that does not contain its own estimate, and the text reads it as fewer symptoms. US sample of 191 (MINI cannabis screening test; no adjustment listed; poor): people who frequently used concentrates did not endorse significantly more symptoms than people who frequently used herbal cannabis (means 2.1 and 1.3); the review notes that the sample endorsed few symptoms overall. These are the only two studies in the review that compare concentrates with herbal cannabis on cannabis use disorder.
results.note: Numbers match Table 2 and Results 12th-13th paragraphs; interval anomaly is real. The -0.05 is for higher-potency concentrate use. 'Only two' holds in the review's terms; the Japanese liquid-or-resin study (OR 6.850) is not called concentrates.

Matches Discussion 2nd, 5th, 8th and 11th paragraphs; refs 36-37 are squirrel monkey self-administration studies, ref 38 treatment entry. No certainty rating anywhere. 'Conclusion' is the closing 'In conclusion' paragraph, not a headed section.

The reference list shows the senior author (T P Freeman) as an author of three of the four cannabis use disorder studies that found an association (the 2015 UK survey, the 2020 175-country survey and the 2020 UK sample, of which review author L Hines is first author); the Japanese study and the two studies that found no association or fewer symptoms are by other groups.

results.corrected_extracted: The review states that concentrate use has been consistently associated with a higher cannabis use disorder risk than other forms; that people who frequently use concentrates show more symptoms than people who do not use them but may also use higher-potency cannabis when not using concentrates (ref. 40, Bidwell et al., 2018, the US sample of 191 that the systematic review reports as showing no significant difference); that people who use concentrates chronically may show more tolerance and withdrawal (ref. 37, Bidwell et al., 2021); that people who regularly use concentrates more often feel worried about their use than people who have tried but do not regularly use them (ref. 42, a national web survey of dab use); and that among college students more frequent use of butane hash oil went with more physical symptoms such as tolerance after adjustment for demographic, substance-use and personality covariates (ref. 43). It gives no effect sizes and calls for longitudinal studies.
results.note: Matches p. 7 paragraph and refs 37, 40, 42, 43; ref. 40 is Petrilli's ref. 29 (191, no significant difference). Inman does not call ref. 37 a review; ref. 42's comparator is people who tried but do not regularly use.

results.corrected_extracted: The review calls the literature on problematic use by form small and incomplete and mostly about flower. It cites a positive association between product potency and cannabis use disorder risk (ref. 52), more symptoms with frequent concentrate use than with frequent flower use (ref. 40), more problematic use with more frequent use of the two inhaled forms but not edibles (ref. 39), and more cannabis use disorder with high-frequency use of all three forms than with high-frequency flower-only use (ref. 15); it says, without a citation, that inhaling is generally linked to a higher risk than swallowing. It concludes that frequency of use remains the most reliable predictor of cannabis use disorder risk across all forms and that further causal factors such as quantity and THC potency are yet to be firmly established. For flower, it cites a cross-sectional survey of 617 Colorado college students in which flower potency was positively associated with symptom count and severity (ref. 36), and says flower's outcomes have rarely been compared with other forms.
results.note: All statements and reference numbers match pp. 6 and 9; the inhalation-versus-ingestion sentence indeed has no citation. Added the design the review gives for the 617-student survey (cross-sectional).

results.corrected_extracted: The review finds limited information specific to the cannabis use disorder potential of edibles. The review argues from studies of other drugs (refs 50 and 51, formulations of hydrocodone and methylphenidate) that a slower onset of action goes with a lower potential to contribute to a substance use disorder, and cites one source (ref. 44, titled as a study of medical cannabis patients with chronic pain) for people who use cannabis medically preferring oral use for symptom relief and for people new to non-medical use or using it infrequently more often than more frequent users naming edibles as their main form. It concludes that the cannabis use disorder outcomes of edibles have not been sufficiently characterised.
results.note: Matches p. 8 CUD outcomes and Conclusion; refs 44, 50, 51 checked. Named the comparator the review gives (higher-frequency users) and the symptom-relief context, and attributed the opening statement to the review.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors found no population study that estimated the risk of cannabis use disorder by the potency of the products used, and mention, without a reference, a Michigan longitudinal study of high-risk families in which people who used higher-potency products had higher risks of developing use-disorder symptoms. Limits they state: heterogeneity, with limited power to detect moderators; 60% of estimates from cross-sectional surveys open to recall bias; lifetime and past-year estimates that differ in meaning (past-year use disorder 15.4% among 18 to 25-year-olds who used that year against 9.8% among those who had ever used, in one US survey); all studies from high-income countries, over half from the US.
results.note: Matches Discussion 7th-9th, 11th and 12th paragraphs; Han figures also match Table 1. The review names it the Michigan Longitudinal Study, so the design is now stated; no reference number is given.
